title: JSON & JSONB Documents and Native Arrays
description: Store, query, and index JSONB documents and native PostgreSQL arrays using operators ->, ->>, @>, and GIN indexing.

data.text: PostgreSQL offers two JSON data types: `JSON` (stored as exact text representation) and **`JSONB`** (decomposed binary format). JSONB is slightly slower to insert because it parses the JSON structure, but provides lightning-fast querying, key lookup, and can be indexed with GIN (Generalized Inverted Index).

data.text: Choose `JSONB` almost always. The only common reason to keep `JSON` is that you must reproduce the exact input bytes (for example, to verify a signature over the original document).

data.text: Arrays are typed, one- or multi-dimensional, and index from 1 — not 0. They are ideal for a small, bounded list (tags, roles) and a poor fit for a one-to-many relation that needs its own attributes.

Do Not Put Large Mutable Documents Behind a GIN Index Without Thinking
data.text: A GIN index makes containment queries fast but every update to the document rewrites index entries (GIN has a pending list to mitigate this, but a hot JSONB row still costs more than a normal update). If you update a document thousands of times a day, project its hot fields into real columns.

data.title: Interview Answer
data.text: Use JSONB when the shape is genuinely dynamic and you mostly query by containment (`@>`) or a few known paths. Promote frequently-filtered keys into real columns with btree indexes — hybrid "document plus columns" designs are the common production answer.

data.title: Model Both Ways and Compare
steps: Create `events` with a raw JSONB payload plus a GIN index.
Create a normalised `events_normalised` with `action TEXT`, `user_id BIGINT`, `tags TEXT[]`.
Write the same three queries against both.
Compare `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` output and the size on disk.
data.expectedOutcome: You can articulate when to normalise and when JSONB is the right call.

items.question: Is JSONB a replacement for MongoDB?
items.answer: For many workloads yes — SQL, transactions, and joins around a document column are usually simpler than running a second database. But JSONB has no per-document schema validation by default (use `CHECK (jsonb_typeof(...))` or a JSON schema validator), and very large documents hit TOAST compression.

items.question: Why did `-` cause a `jsonb - text` vs `jsonb - text[]` ambiguity for me?
items.answer: Because both operators exist. Cast explicitly: `payload - 'key'` removes a key, `payload - ARRAY['a','b']` removes several, `payload - 1` removes an array element.

items.question: How do I validate JSONB shape?
items.answer: Add a `CHECK` constraint (for example `CHECK (jsonb_typeof(payload) = 'object')`) or use the `jsonb_matches_schema()` function from the `pg_jsonschema`/`is_jsonb_valid` extension.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Always prefer `JSONB` over plain `JSON` for production querying.
Use GIN indexes with the containment operator `@>` for sub-millisecond document queries.
